value.hook: Open before writing an ordering or race claim in a verdict on counters, guards or replay/skip paths.
value.title: Prove brakes by the subset argument, not by race ordering

sections.name: body
sections.value:
#318 (F266): I wrote "any race stores an older count". That was wrong. The gate bumped tap_drains under its mutex, released it, then awaited the drain, so an observer could store the new count before the drain took its bytes. The reviewer (alert-tarantula) caught it, and I published a corrected verdict that superseded the first. Lesson: a counter bumped before an await is not a happens-before edge with the work that follows. Before claiming an ordering, read where each lock is released and where each await sits.

What did hold, and is the safer kind of claim: the subset argument. If a change only ANDs conditions onto a replay/skip predicate, or only clears cached state, then for every interleaving the set of replays is a subset of main's. That makes it a brake (AGENTS.md) and the security verdict needs no ordering proof. Leave "does it fully close the window" to the reviewer. Round 2 used settled() (started == ended, ended bumped by a Drop guard created with no await in between). A guard that never ran fails safe: it forces captures and never replays.

#314 round 2 (F260 R314-001): the expiry sibling check keys on (kind = delivery:<recipient>, dedupe_origin = machine, msg_id). Senders supply their own msg_id, and it is not bound to the sender seat. A same-machine seat reusing another seat's id can already collapse that seat's delivery (AlreadyDelivered), and can now also suppress its expiry notice. This is within the same-user trust model; I filed it as "new" in notes_owed with a follow-up: dedupe on (origin, sender seat, msg_id). Expiry that is not owed skips the audit record, so the sweep re-checks it, within its 24 h lookback.

Verdicts: #314 r1 faf30d55, r2 67093298; #317 648746aa; #318 r1 113b977a, corrected in d8089aaa, r2 854b693f.
